subject: mcc-professional-behaviours
title: Documentation and records: accurate, auditable, and safe

steps.tx: Medical records are a **legal and clinical account** of what happened and why decisions were made. Every entry should be accurate, timely, signed and attributable to its author. Records are read by colleagues who may act on them tomorrow, so an error left uncorrected can harm a patient. Good documentation is a core professional duty, and a poor record can be as damaging as poor care. Remember that the chart should describe facts, not blame.
steps.say: Medical records are a legal and clinical account of what happened and why decisions were made. Every entry should be accurate, timely, signed and attributable to its author. Records are read by colleagues who may act on them tomorrow, so an uncorrected error can harm a patient. Good documentation is a core professional duty. Remember that the chart should describe facts, not blame.

steps.tx: When an entry is wrong, correct it without erasing it. Draw a single line through the error, so it remains legible, then add the **correct value**, the date, your initials or identity, and a brief reason. Never delete, overwrite or back-date an entry. This keeps an **audit trail**, so anyone reviewing the record can see what changed, when, and by whom. Erasure removes the trail and looks like tampering.

rows: Strike through with initials, date and reason

steps.tx: A **late entry** is the right way to document something you forgot to write at the time. Label it clearly as a late entry, state the date and time you are writing it, and state the actual date of the event it describes. Do not pretend it was written earlier. A call or decision made yesterday but recorded today should show both dates. This keeps the timeline honest and lets readers judge how reliable the entry is.

steps.tx: Verbal and telephone communications are high risk. For a **verbal order**, use read-back: repeat the order to the prescriber, confirm it was heard correctly, and document the prescriber name, time and content. For a **critical result** phoned to you, record who called, the time, the result, and that it was read back. Verbal information must always be captured in writing so that it can be acted on and reviewed later.

steps.tx: Access to records and incident reporting need care. A **capable adult** controls access to their own information, so a relative needs the patient's consent or another lawful basis before receiving it. A competent patient can request a copy of their chart; **third-party information** about other people may be redacted. Record facts of an adverse event, such as dose, blood pressure change, timing and recovery, in the chart. Keep speculation about cause and blame out of the record, and file a separate **incident report** for system review.

steps.tx: Each **capacity** assessment should be recorded for the specific decision at hand, because ability can vary over time and between choices. The patient needs to **grasp** the facts, **weigh** how they bear on their own circumstances, compare the realistic routes forward, and state a clear preference. A medical condition, advanced years or a relative's objection do not, on their own, justify concluding that someone cannot choose. When a clinician reaches that view, the notes should set out the reasoning and the steps taken to reach it.
